title: Confession and Verdict
premise: Yara Okonkwo, a retired detective who faked her death to escape a corrupt precinct, receives a confession letter for a drowning ruled accidental fifteen years ago—postmarked the day after the victim's mother finally stopped waiting. The letter names a second victim the police never found, and its writer is being hunted by the same men Yara once called colleagues. As Yara investigates alongside the victim's estranged daughter and her bookshop's ragtag regulars, she must decide whether exposing the truth is worth burning the new life she built. The case ends at the tidal flats where the second body surfaces, the corrupt former chief is arrested, and Yara—her identity exposed—chooses to stand trial as herself rather than vanish again.
about_author: Ulyana Nakamura is a former court stenographer who spent eleven years transcribing testimony before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries from a coastal town where the fog rolls in earlier every year.

chapters.title: The Postmark
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Three weeks after closing her bookshop early to avoid a funeral, Yara finds a confession letter in the morning mail—postmarked the day after the burial. The writer admits to witnessing a drowning fifteen years ago and claims it was no accident. The beat is dread: the past has her address.

chapters.title: Closed for Good
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. She researches the case: Teodora Voss, drowned off Gull Point, ruled accidental, case sealed by then-Sergeant Merrick Hale—Yara's former mentor. Yara burns the letter in the shop's stove, then retrieves it, half-charred, from the ash. The beat is denial curdling into compulsion.

chapters.title: The Daughter Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Nadia Voss's POV. Nadia, the dead woman's estranged daughter, arrives at the bookshop asking if anyone's written to her too—she's received a page torn from a tide log. Yara lies badly. The beat is wary connection between two women circling the same wound.

chapters.title: Regulars
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Her found family surfaces: Felix, the insomniac ex-journalist who runs the crossword table; Marisol, the teenage clerk who reads the returns; Old Piet, who fishes the flats. Yara asks Piet, too casually, what the tide gives back after fifteen years. The beat is the warmth she's been hiding inside.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Piet's POV. Piet remembers the night Teodora died—he saw a boat with two men aboard, and a third man on the rocks who never got wet. He never told police because the man on the rocks was Hale. The beat is the heavy cost of a silence kept too long.

chapters.title: The Second Victim
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The confession letter's postscript mentions 'the one in the boathouse,' a victim never reported missing. Yara cross-references missing persons from that winter and finds Dario Lenz, a dockworker whose file was purged. The beat is the cold realization the confession writer knows things only a killer—or the killer's witness—could know.

chapters.title: Someone Is Reading My Mail
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. The bookshop is searched while she's at the archive; nothing stolen but the letter's envelope is gone. She finds a tide chart pinned behind the register with Gull Point circled in red. The beat is fear becoming personal—the writer isn't confessing to her, they're using her.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years Invisible
chapters.summary: Yara's POV, flashback-woven. Nadia presses her on how she knows police procedure so well, and Yara reveals fragments of the truth: she testified against the precinct, was declared dead in a staged accident, and rebuilt herself here. The beat is vulnerability traded for trust—Nadia stays anyway.

chapters.title: The Writer's Hand
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix, who spent decades verifying sources, analyzes the letter: the handwriting shifts midway—the second half written by someone else, or by someone whose hand was shaking. He recognizes the stationery as old precinct issue. The beat is the puzzle deepening into something uglier.

chapters.title: Hale Comes Ashore
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Merrick Hale, now retired and decorated, walks into the bookshop buying a paperback on maritime law. He knows who she is—or who she was. He warns her, gently, that some verdicts are load-bearing. The beat is polite menace; the reader's skin crawls.

chapters.title: Marisol's Discovery
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Shelving returns, Marisol finds a hollowed-out book—Yara's old case notes hidden years ago—missing the pages on the Lenz file. She tells Yara, terrified she's in trouble. The beat is found family under pressure: Marisol chooses loyalty over self-preservation.

chapters.title: The Boathouse
chapters.summary: Yara and Nadia's alternating POV. They search the derelict boathouse at Gull Point and find a wall cavity with Dario Lenz's watch and a child's drawing—Nadia's own, from the winter her mother died. The beat is grief detonating: the second victim was killed because he saw what happened to Teodora.

chapters.title: Confession, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. They trace the letter's writer to a hospice: Brother Anselm, once Father Anselm, the priest who took Teodora's final confession and has been dying slowly for a decade. But when they arrive, his room is empty and his nurse is dead. The beat is the race turning lethal.

chapters.title: What Anselm Knew
chapters.summary: Anselm's POV, a letter he wrote to be opened after his death. He heard Teodora's confession—that she witnessed Hale and a councilman moving contraband through the harbor—and gave her absolution instead of protection. Hale found out. The beat is the terrible arithmetic of a good man's cowardice.

chapters.title: The Trap at the Flats
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara realizes the tide chart and stolen envelope were bait: Hale needs her to find Lenz's body before the spring dredging erases it, so he can control what surfaces. She lets him believe she's taking the bait. The beat is the hunter reversing the hunt.

chapters.title: Low Tide
chapters.summary: Yara, Nadia, and Piet's POV in rotation. Under cover of a storm surge, the three search the flats and find Lenz's remains weighted under a mooring stone—along with Hale's old badge, planted to frame a dead man. Yara photographs everything and hides the originals. The beat is grim triumph shadowed by exposure.

chapters.title: Burned
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Hale's men torch the bookshop that night. Marisol, sleeping in the loft, is pulled out by Felix. Standing in the ash, Yara finds her own staged-death certificate pinned to the door. The beat is the price arriving all at once—her invisibility is over.

chapters.title: Verdict Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Nadia's POV. Nadia confronts Hale at a harbor fundraiser with a recording of his warning at the bookshop, while Felix feeds the evidence to a state investigative reporter. Hale realizes the net is closing and goes for the flats himself, to destroy what the tide holds. The beat is civilian courage against institutional power.

chapters.title: Gull Point
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Climax. Yara intercepts Hale on the rocks at slack tide. He offers her the old bargain—disappear, and the file stays buried. She refuses, and when his man moves to kill them both, Piet's boat light and the arriving state police end it. Hale is arrested on the flats where his victims drowned. The beat is justice chosen over survival.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara walks into the state attorney's office and gives her real name for the first time in fifteen years, surrendering to face her own old charges so her evidence will hold. The beat is the theme made flesh: justice outside the law only counts if she walks back inside it.

chapters.title: What the Tide Gives Up
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Teodora and Dario are reburied under their true names; Anselm's letter becomes the state's centerpiece. Yara, out on her own recognizance, watches the verdicts from the gallery—Hale convicted, the councilman flipped, the precinct's seal finally broken. The beat is grief finding its shape in public truth.

chapters.title: Reopening Day
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Spring. The bookshop reopens, rebuilt by the regulars, a new tide log on the counter where customers record what the water returned. Nadia works the register; Marisol has her own key. A stranger leaves an envelope—inside, a thank-you note and no threat. Yara, for the first time, signs her real name in the log. The beat is found family and a self, reclaimed.
